During training, EOS is treated as another token without a special loss term or incentive. Although this training paradigm is widely used, it is not understood how models decide to output EOS. We study a minimal version of the EOS halting problem in which networks are trained to emit a given input sequence an instructed number of times, followed by EOS. We train tanh RNNs and linear SSMs on this task, finding that the RNNs encode the number of tokens left to copy in a linear subspace, of which two principal components capture most of the variation. Hidden states with the same remaining count converge to a shared representation regardless of their instructed repeat count. By modulating the hidden state using an affine transformation at the boundary between copied sequences, we shift the RNN's state to the representation shared by states with one fewer copy remaining. The unchanged network emits EOS one copy earlier while reproducing the shortened target sequence in 94.4% of new sequences, revealing that this representation causally determines the stopping time. In the SSMs, the difference between trajectories with different repeat counts is separated across two-dimensional rotation planes whose contributions to the EOS comparison cancel during copying and align near the stopping time. Rotating the planes independently removes most of the intended stopping while preserving the copied content, which shows that the stopping time depends on the planes' relative phases. These results identify two candidate primitives of EOS halting in recurrent models: a shared encoding of the number of remaining tokens in tanh RNNs and phase alignment across fixed rotations in linear SSMs.
core_methodology: Investigates how recurrent sequence models (RNNs and SSMs) decide to output an end-of-sequence (EOS) token, focusing on minimal halting problems in controlled settings.
data_sources: Synthetic sequences designed to test EOS halting behavior, not market or financial data.
alpha_potential: Limited direct application to trading; mainly theoretical insights into sequence modeling that could inform future model designs.

title: JointQ: Joint Scale-and-Integer Quantization for Large Language Models
summary: GPTQ is the de facto standard solver for layer-wise post-training quantization (PTQ) of large language models, yet the solver itself has received less attention than weight preprocessing and cross-layer objectives. We target a bottleneck of GPTQ: its greedy procedure optimizes continuous group scales separately from the assignment of discrete integers. Evaluating each integer candidate with its closed-form optimal scale has been used for per-channel quantization; JointQ extends it to group-wise quantization, where a row's scales are coupled through the Hessian, and applies it to refine the GPTQ solution. Each local-search move changes one integer and recomputes its group's optimal scale in closed form, accounting for the other groups through the full Hessian; all scales are periodically re-solved jointly. The search starts from a row-wise selection among scale-refitted candidates including the GPTQ solution, so unregularized JointQ never has a larger layer-wise calibration error than GPTQ. JointQ preserves the GPTQ output format and is thus a drop-in replacement. Across four models and four settings, JointQ improves six-task average zero-shot accuracy over vanilla GPTQ in 14 of 16 comparisons and perplexity in 12 of 16. The mean accuracy gain increases from 0.0044 in W4G128 to 0.1559 in W3 per-channel, and JointQ also improves average accuracy over GPTQ with MSE-based scale search and activation ordering in all eight per-channel comparisons, though rarely in G128. An ablation shows that JointQ's diagonal Tikhonov regularization mitigates severe W3 per-channel perplexity degradation, so the largest gains are not due to the local search alone. Overall, JointQ's primary empirical benefit is downstream accuracy preservation in challenging low-bit and large-group regimes. Code is available in the OneComp library at https://github.com/FujitsuResearch/OneCompression.
core_methodology: Joint scale-and-integer quantization for large language models, improving upon GPTQ by jointly optimizing scales and integers with local search and closed-form solutions
data_sources: Not specified (general LLM quantization research)
alpha_potential: Potential for more efficient deployment of LLMs in trading systems, but no direct trading application demonstrated

title: Regularizing Treatment Leakage for LLM-based Uplift Estimation
summary: Uplift modeling estimates the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) and supports industrial decisions such as promotional pricing. When large language models (LLMs) encode product text, treatment-revealing content can introduce shortcuts that do not transfer to deployment. We propose \emph{LLM-based Uplift Leakage Regularization} (\textsc{LULR}), which uses a CLUB-based penalty on the causal head's trainable shared representation while keeping the LLM encoder frozen. Controlled proxy experiments show a positive ranking-score interaction and higher scores than the tested weight-decay configuration; treatment-dependent evaluation limits their interpretation to exploratory model behavior. Structured-only comparisons provide reference performance, without establishing a general advantage over tree-based estimators. On a million-record industrial pricing RCT, \textsc{LULR} improves offline $\text{lift@}0.3$ in $4/5$ seeds, although the difference is not statistically significant and estimated policy values are near-tied. A separate one-week online A/B experiment records $5.45\%$ higher sales volume and $1.91\%$ higher GMV than the control arm. These aggregate results provide short-term business evidence for the complete deployed pricing policy; they do not isolate the regularizer's contribution.
core_methodology: LLM-based Uplift Leakage Regularization (LULR) for estimating Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) in promotional pricing scenarios
data_sources: Industrial pricing RCT (Randomized Controlled Trial) data and product text
alpha_potential: Potential for improving promotional pricing strategies by better estimating treatment effects, though not directly applicable to trading

title: Auditing World-Model Explanations in Retail Forecasting: Faithfulness, Accuracy and Price Response
summary: Forecasting models that read the price and promotion plan explain each forecast as a baseline, what would sell with nothing planned, plus the lift the plan adds. We test such explanations with eight checks, six with a pass rule fixed before any result, and find that passing them does not make an explanation right. In generated store data with known effects, a world model passes the checks of construction, stability, price direction and agreement with sales and with LightGBM, yet its lifts are 1.33 to 1.40 times the truth when merchants plan into high-demand weeks, and 1.23 to 1.42 times in eight variants of that world. It still picks the right weeks to promote, but stock ordered to its lift is off by 0.44 to 0.48 of the true lift. Its stated response to a lasting regular-price change is 4.7 to 6.5 times the true -0.5, and only a measured cause finds this. On Dominick's, 38 episodes in which a store's regular prices sat apart from its zone peers give a noisy benchmark: a pooled 8-week response of -0.33 (95% interval -0.68 to 0.01). For the final tuned world models of our companion paper on nine data sets, baseline and lift add up under each model's own plan, but a deeper price cut lowers the forecast in 29% to 83% of item-week steps on Dominick's (23% to 80% within prices seen in training), and the world model and LightGBM both state about twice the measured response. Across 703 configurations from the settings searches, checks passed were not related to forecast accuracy (Spearman 0.02, 95% interval -0.02 to 0.05); with no known answer for those versions, this concerns accuracy, while whether an explanation is right is measured only in the generated data.
core_methodology: Auditing world-model explanations in retail forecasting through faithfulness and accuracy checks
data_sources: Generated store data with known effects and Dominick's dataset (retail store data)
alpha_potential: Limited direct alpha potential; focuses on model explanation auditing rather than predictive signal generation

title: Same Fix, Different Weights: Replicating Weight-Space Programming with Claude
summary: Takehi et al. (2026) report that GPT-6 Astra, given the weights of small neural networks as text, can say what they were trained to do, repair them, and write new ones without training. I re-ran the core of that study with Claude Opus 5.5 in ten pre-registered experiments, with untrained-network and permutation controls and hand audits of every sandboxed code cell. Reading was mixed: Claude named 3 of 4 Atari games from policy weights and found the measured copying heads in 15/15 character-LM runs, but its answers about training data often followed priors. Unlike the original, it identified a sycophantic Gemma 3 270M finetune from weights alone in 6/6 runs. One-shot weight edits took a failing MountainCar policy from 0% to 100% success and a hovering LunarLander policy from 0% to 85.6%; zero-shot networks beat PPO at 100k steps on 4 of 5 environments, each implementing a textbook controller. With no training or forward passes, Claude wrote a 1.48M-parameter 9x9 Go network that won 85-94% of games against three PPO opponents. Given Qwen3.5-0.8B's weights and 10, 25 or 50 forward passes of 64 practice problems, Claude raised MATH-500 from 6.7% to 51.4%, 55.2% and 58.1% (+51.4 points at 50 passes, 95% CI [47.9, 55.0]; original 48.1%), GSM8K from 11.6% to 68.2% and IFEval from 22.2% to 54.2%. Unlike the original, which removed an internal loop direction, every edit acted at the output: it scaled the final norm, raising the effective sampling temperature, and lowered the logit of "Wait" while raising that of </think>. The norm scaling alone reaches only 20.9-22.1% on MATH-500. On Gemma 3 270M, which rarely loops, no edit helped (-0.8 points), as in the original.
core_methodology: Investigates the capability of LLMs (Claude Opus 5.5) to interpret, modify, and generate neural network weights without training, focusing on performance in various control tasks and game environments.
data_sources: Neural network weights from small networks, performance metrics from control tasks (MountainCar, LunarLander) and game environments (9x9 Go), and benchmark datasets (MATH-500, GSM8K, IFEval).
alpha_potential: Potential for automated model optimization and adaptation without retraining, but direct financial application is unclear. Could be relevant for adaptive trading systems if applied to financial models.

title: FH-Sampling: Frequency-aware Hypergraph-driven Oversampling for Imbalanced Time-Series Classification
summary: Imbalanced time-series data appears commonly in diverse applications, such as medical diagnosis. When trained on imbalanced data, classifiers tend to exhibit a bias toward the majority class, making it difficult to identify minority-class instances accurately, despite their critical importance. Sampling techniques have proven effective in rebalancing imbalanced data. However, existing interpolation-based oversampling methods typically rely on pairwise interpolation, limiting their ability to capture high-order inter-sample relationships, and their inherent smoothing effects tend to suppress high-frequency components, compromising spectral fidelity. Therefore, we propose a Frequency-aware Hypergraph-driven Oversampling method (FH-Sampling) for imbalanced time-series classification. In FH-Sampling, a hypergraph is first constructed in the original time-series space to capture complex high-order inter-sample relationships, and sampling ratios are adaptively assigned to mitigate the impact of noisy samples. The discrete wavelet transform decomposes each sample into frequency components. Guided by the sample hypergraph, FH-Sampling combines high-frequency components from related samples while retaining the target sample's low-frequency component to help preserve important frequency characteristics. Experiments on 24 imbalanced datasets demonstrate the advantages of FH-Sampling for imbalanced time-series classification. We further apply FH-Sampling to aircraft trajectory generation. Experiments on simulated aircraft trajectories show that FH-Sampling produces trajectories that better match the real distribution, highlighting its potential for practical applications.
core_methodology: Frequency-aware Hypergraph-driven Oversampling method (FH-Sampling) for imbalanced time-series classification, utilizing hypergraphs for high-order inter-sample relationships and discrete wavelet transforms for frequency component decomposition
data_sources: Primarily tested on imbalanced time-series datasets, with an application example on simulated aircraft trajectories
alpha_potential: Potential applications in detecting rare events in financial time-series data (e.g., flash crashes, fraud detection), but direct trading applications not demonstrated

title: The Price of Choosing Examples: Context Overfitting in Adaptive In-Context Learning
summary: In-context learning is usually analyzed as if the examples in the prompt were sampled before the learner is chosen. In deployed systems they are not: examples are retrieved, filtered, re-ranked, edited, and repeatedly tested after seeing the query and the data store. We formalize this gap by treating prompt construction as adaptive data analysis through a conditional stochastic-kernel calculus. Our main quantity is the context capacity, the mutual information or approximate max-information between the data store and the final prompt transcript. For any frozen in-context learner and any adaptive context pipeline with capacity $\kappa$, we prove a finite-sample context generalization bound of order $\sqrt{\kappa/k}$, where $k$ is the number of selected examples whose losses form the reported score. We prove a matching lower bound, whose constant is exact when $\log k\ll\kappa\ll k$, and derive two PAC-Bayesian retrieval rules: a first-order Gibbs rule that charges data-dependent candidate gates their prior mass, and a self-normalized second-order rule. On Banking77 with 64 retrieval recipes and two model families, the certificates hold in all 24,000 resampled selection events, and from 64 (Qwen2.5-7B) or 128 (GPT-4.1-mini) reused validation queries the Gibbs rule certifies a risk below the zero-shot error in over 99% of validation draws. Finally, we instantiate the theory for Bayesian linear in-context regression, including an order-statistics analysis of query-aligned top-$k$ Gaussian retrieval. The results separate context quality from context certification: longer or more relevant contexts improve risk only when the procedure used to choose them is stable enough for selected-context evidence to transfer.
core_methodology: Adaptive in-context learning with context capacity analysis
data_sources: Banking77 dataset, validation queries with GPT-related models
alpha_potential: Potentially useful for improving information retrieval in AI-driven financial context selection, but no direct market application demonstrated

title: Tensorized Automata: Algebraically Informed Representation Learning for Sequential Decision Making
summary: Task representations for sequential decision making should describe both an objective and progress toward it. We present an algebraically informed pipeline that uses the relational structure and language semantics of alternating finite automata (AFAs) to learn control features and compile compact execution operators. AND-OR message passing learns task and state vectors; selected configurations define an event-driven Boolean matrix operator. We prove that initial and successor language coverage make its carrier represent the exact residual after every prefix, with a sufficient capacity bound in terms of reachable configurations. Conjunction and disjunction use the same pipeline. Fidelity and composition audits evaluate copied formulas and learned disjunct assignments. In five-policy-seed XLand experiments with larger training pools, pooled execution-state vectors outperform raw carrier bits and task-blind conditioning across three task pools under two rejection rewards. They achieve 77.3\% success on multi-event tasks and 99.4\% on a four-task stratum with 33--128-state minimal DFAs, using 16 operator slots. LetterWorld results show useful residual conditioning alongside a remaining gap to RAD. These results connect algebraically informed representation learning to compact task execution and useful policy conditioning.
core_methodology: Utilizes algebraically informed representation learning with alternating finite automata (AFAs) for sequential decision making, focusing on task representation and execution operators.
data_sources: Experimental results from XLand and LetterWorld tasks, not financial market data.
alpha_potential: Potential indirect application in algorithmic trading for sequential decision-making tasks, but requires significant adaptation to financial contexts.

title: Averaged-Cost Control with Shared Feedback under Model Uncertainty
summary: This paper studies the shared-feedback design problem for finite-horizon averaged-cost control under model uncertainty represented by a joint law over the model parameter and initial state. One feedback map is shared across all realizations and uses only time and the current state as online inputs. We develop two methods: the nonlinear adjoint method combines forward closed-loop solves, backward adjoints, and joint-law policy gradients, while the linear moment method gives exact cost and gradient formulas for a homogeneous linear-quadratic design model by propagating conditional second moments. Numerical studies compare averaged and nominal designs for time-dependent neural feedback and static linear feedback in nonlinear Van der Pol and Stuart-Landau systems; the static gains are designed from oscillator linearizations and evaluated on the original nonlinear systems. Averaged design has lower cost in most comparisons.
core_methodology: Shared-feedback design for averaged-cost control under model uncertainty using nonlinear adjoint and linear moment methods
data_sources: Model parameters and initial state distributions (not market data)
alpha_potential: Potential application in optimal execution or portfolio rebalancing under uncertainty, but requires significant adaptation to financial markets

title: Interpreting Random Forests: Comparing Surrogate Models and Rule Extraction Methods
summary: Random forests (RFs) often achieve high prediction performance, but their ensemble structure can be difficult to interpret. Surrogate models and rule extraction methods offer interpretable approximations, yet guidance on selecting an appropriate method for a specific research question remains limited. We compared 12 methods for interpreting RFs, with a decision tree as a prediction-oriented reference, across 11 simulation settings and 67 benchmark datasets for regression and classification. Evaluation addressed prediction and structural similarity to the RF, model complexity, prediction performance, and runtime. Simulations additionally assessed explainability using known effect and noise variables. No method performed best across all objectives. For regression, SLIM provided the strongest general performance for prediction similarity or performance on test data, while a linear model offered a simpler global interpretation of linear effects when performance was comparable. For classification, inTrees achieved the strongest overall benchmark performance, with CTree and OC-CART providing useful alternatives. ART consistently produced the most compact representations. NH and SIRUS offered strong structural similarity for regression, while MRT most closely reproduced RF variable usage in the classification simulations, illustrating that prediction-oriented rankings do not necessarily identify the best structural explanation. Outcome-type restrictions, runtime limits, and method-specific failures reduced result availability for several approaches and should be considered alongside performance when selecting a method. Method selection should therefore be guided by the outcome type, anticipated data structure, and intended interpretability objective. Prediction similarity alone is insufficient for explaining an RF and should be considered jointly with structural similarity and model complexity.
core_methodology: Comparison of interpretability methods for random forests including surrogate models and rule extraction techniques
data_sources: Simulation settings and 67 benchmark datasets for regression and classification (non-financial)
alpha_potential: Potential for improving model interpretability in trading strategies, though not directly demonstrated with financial data

title: Steering Bayesian Inference and Decisions through Data Poisoning
summary: Adversarial machine learning has revealed that statistical models can be manipulated through poisoned data, and Bayesian inference is no exception. Earlier work has shown that subtle poisoning attacks can drive the posterior toward a distribution of the attacker's choosing. Such posterior attraction attacks require a fully specified target posterior; however, attackers typically care about only a few posterior quantities or, more consequentially, about a downstream decision. Herein, we study how an attacker can alter Bayesian inference and decisions by deleting or replicating a few observations, chosen to minimize the maximum mean discrepancy between the resulting posterior and a target distribution. A suitable kernel lets the attacker steer selected posterior moments without specifying the rest of the target. Because Bayes actions depend on the posterior only through expected utilities, which are themselves posterior moments, the same approach can target a decision directly. We construct the attacks with a gradient-based heuristic that requires only posterior samples, and analyze its convergence. Experiments with regression and hierarchical models compare moment-based and full-posterior attacks, and illustrate how deleting a handful of observations can flip a Bayesian decision.
core_methodology: Gradient-based heuristic for data poisoning attacks on Bayesian inference, focusing on altering posterior moments and decisions through selective data deletion/replication
data_sources: General statistical models (tested on regression/hierarchical models), not financial-specific
alpha_potential: Potential defensive applications for detecting model manipulation in quantitative finance, but no direct trading signal generation

title: Joint Learning of Factual and Counterfactual Worlds for Causal Prior-data Fitted Networks
summary: Estimating treatment effects is central to science across many disciplines and requires counterfactual reasoning about alternative worlds. In the real world, however, each unit reveals its outcome only under the factual world. Thus, the factual and counterfactual outcomes can never be jointly learned by any model trained on real data. The problem is therefore tractable only in synthetic settings, where both worlds can be generated. Recent progress on prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) has shown that models pre-trained purely on synthetic data can transfer to real-world prediction. This paradigm has since carried over to causal effect estimation. Despite this fully synthetic setup, existing causal PFNs carry the real-world constraint into their training objective, confining learning to a single world's outcome per unit. The dependence between the two worlds is thereby lost, and the density of the treatment effect relies by default on independence, which is implausible in practice. We therefore propose joint learning, a training setup in which a causal PFN learns the joint distribution of the factual and counterfactual outcomes of each unit. From the joint distribution, we obtain both the response and the individual treatment effect densities, and at inference, we apply optimal transport across units to obtain an approximation of the average treatment effect density. Ours is therefore the first causal PFN approach to provide all three densities together while accounting for the cross-world dependence. We apply joint learning and optimal transport to existing causal PFNs and evaluate it across semi-synthetic, synthetic, and real benchmarks spanning diverse causal scenarios. The jointly trained models significantly improve upon their baselines in point estimation and uncertainty quantification in most settings, indicating that joint learning is a preferable training setup for causal PFNs.
core_methodology: Joint learning of factual and counterfactual outcomes using prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) with optimal transport for treatment effect estimation
data_sources: Synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets, possibly real-world data for validation
alpha_potential: Potential for identifying causal relationships in financial scenarios, but lacks direct market data applications

title: Relax-and-Sparsify Approximation Algorithms for Sparse Ridge Regression
summary: This paper studies sparse ridge regression in the low-rank, high-dimensional setting that often arises when data collection is expensive. By exploiting the low-rank structure, we develop approximation algorithms within a relax-and-sparsify framework: solve a convex relaxation and then sparsify its solution to satisfy the original sparsity constraint. Specifically, we establish a tight rank-dependent sparsity bound for the convex relaxation by decomposing its support into two parts. This decomposition in turn motivates two approximation strategies, parameter reduction and binary redistribution, each exploiting a different part. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that the binary redistribution algorithms outperform the benchmarks in most instances.
core_methodology: Relax-and-Sparsify approximation framework for sparse ridge regression with two strategies: parameter reduction and binary redistribution
data_sources: Synthetic and real datasets (non-financial)
alpha_potential: Potential application in sparse factor models or high-dimensional portfolio optimization, but requires adaptation for financial data

title: Markets for Compute and Inference: Structure, Financing, and Risk Transfer
summary: Capacity to run large language models is rented by the accelerator-hour, and their output is sold by the million tokens. Both goods now have published price indices, an over-the-counter forward has traded on one, a perpetual future on one is listed offshore, and CME and ICE have specified futures on rental indices that await the United States regulator. We ask what in these two markets can be hedged, by whom, and at what price. Three findings stand out. First, the price that exchange contracts settle on is not the price that drives operators' revenue. Every contract references the published short-dated rental rate, while most revenue, and with it credit quality, comes from private multi-year contracts whose prices are largely undisclosed. Second, the token price and the rental rate are linked by an identity through throughput and margin, but they are different exposures, so a hedge on the rental rate does not hedge the cost of inference; at the measured capability of GPT-5 the cheapest list price fell by a factor of 17 in twelve months, and by far less at lower capability. Third, the demand for hedging already sits in credit agreements, as the years by which operators' debt outlives their contracted revenue. Filings cannot measure that gap, because debt is scheduled year by year while contracted revenue rarely is, and the one loan that prices it settles the risk by cash prepayment against a model only the parties see. We design a reverse convertible note through which leveraged operators could buy protection against falling rental rates. Its coupon depends steeply on the annualised volatility of the rental rate, which the two public indices put between about 5% and 89% according to how each is built and the horizon measured; across that range the fair one-year coupon runs from 4.1% to 31.5%.
core_methodology: Analysis of hedging mechanisms and financial instruments in compute and inference markets
data_sources: Published price indices for accelerator-hours and tokens, private contracts, and credit agreements
alpha_potential: Potential for hedging strategies in compute rental markets, but limited direct application to traditional financial markets

title: Measuring Coherence in Predictive Models
summary: Many sequential decision-making procedures, such as active learning, implicitly assume that a model's current predictions agree with those it expects to make after updating on new data, a property we call coherence. Most models in use do not update by exact conditioning and are not guaranteed to be coherent, which can lead to worse decisions. Yet there is currently no general way to measure incoherence or to tell when it matters. We develop tools to measure incoherence and characterise when it affects decisions. We introduce the incoherence ratio, an MMD-based measure of how far any updating procedure departs from coherence, computed only from the procedure's own predictions and updates, and accompany it with an anytime-valid test of coherence. In Bayesian experimental design, acquisition objectives that are equivalent for coherent models choose different data under every approximate model we study, and the incoherence ratio tracks how far incoherence distorts them. We also introduce action coherence, which captures only the incoherence that changes a decision. What a resulting disagreement costs, however, is determined primarily by predictive accuracy. Sequential decisions depend on how a model updates as well as on what it predicts, so coherence, like accuracy, should be checked rather than assumed.
core_methodology: Measurement of model coherence in sequential decision-making using MMD-based incoherence ratio and anytime-valid coherence testing
data_sources: General model prediction outputs (domain agnostic)
alpha_potential: Limited direct trading applications - potentially useful for validating model stability in reinforcement learning trading frameworks

title: Generative Data Augmentation Without External Data: An Empirical and Theoretical Study on Deep Networks
summary: Generative data augmentation adds samples from generative models to a classifier's training set. Many influential studies use generators pre-trained on large external datasets, and so mix the value of synthetic data with knowledge transferred through pretraining. We study the case without external data, where each generator learns only from the classifier's own training set, and ask when and why adding generated samples to that training set raises or lowers the classifier's test accuracy. We train classifiers with four backbones on six datasets, two of them medical, adding samples from four generators. We bound the excess risk of a classifier trained with synthetic data, that is, how far its population risk can lie above the minimum risk within its hypothesis class. The bound charges synthetic data for the total variation distance between the real and generated distributions and credits synthetic data for a larger training set. The gain from adding synthetic data, the fall in population risk, is at most the excess risk of the real-only classifier, which trains on the real images alone. Read through the bound, the experiments suggest that synthetic data help most when our classifiers detect only a small discrepancy between the generated and real data and the real-only classifier has room to improve, and that synthetic data help little or hurt when the detected discrepancy is large. Generators with a larger lower bound on the total variation distance, a bound that we estimate from our own classifiers, tend to help less on five of the six datasets, and on the CIFAR datasets the most accurate backbone gains the least. The bound gives these directions but not the size of the largest gains, most of which traditional augmentation also reaches at the same number of optimizer steps.
core_methodology: Generative data augmentation using synthetic samples from models trained only on the classifier's own training set, without external data
data_sources: Six datasets including two medical datasets and CIFAR datasets
alpha_potential: Potential to improve model robustness in limited data scenarios, but direct financial application unclear

title: Training Multi-Layer Over-Parametrized Neural Network in Subquadratic Time
summary: We consider the problem of training the last layer of a multi-layer over-parametrized neural network to minimize the empirical risk induced by a loss function. In the typical setting of over-parametrization, the network width $m$ is much larger than the data dimension $d$ and the number of training samples $n$ ($m=\mathrm{poly}(n,d)$), which induces a prohibitively large weight matrix $W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}$ per layer above the first. Naively, when the layer inputs are dense, one has to pay $O(m^2)$ time to read the weight matrix and evaluate the neural network function in both forward and backward computation. To reduce the training cost per iteration, we propose a framework that uses $O(m^2nL)$ time in the initialization phase and achieves a truly subquadratic amortized cost per iteration in terms of $m$, i.e., $m^{2-\Omega(1)}$ per iteration. The speedup comes from a sparse activation, a shifted ReLU whose threshold at each layer is proportional to the norm of the layer input. With this threshold every layer is positively homogeneous, so our convergence proof needs a width only polynomial in the depth $L$, in $n$ and in the inverse smallest kernel eigenvalues. The inputs of the trained layer are fixed and sparse. In this setting, simpler algorithms without a data structure reach the same cost per iteration, and maintaining the products of the last layer with its inputs lowers it to $mn^{\omega-1+o(1)}$, where $\omega$ is the matrix multiplication exponent. Our result can be viewed as an idealized model of maintaining a small amount of state on top of a frozen pre-trained model to speed up fine-tuning, a core procedure to deploy large language models (LLMs). Our guarantees assume that the frozen layers are random, and for a pre-trained model only the cost per iteration of maintaining these products carries over.
core_methodology: Proposes a framework for training over-parametrized neural networks with subquadratic time complexity using sparse activations and shifted ReLU
data_sources: Not specified (theoretical paper)
alpha_potential: Potential for faster training of large neural networks, which could be adapted for financial time series prediction, but no direct trading application demonstrated

title: Linear-time Rule Mining Under Formal Guarantees
summary: Probabilistic logical models are a core component of neurosymbolic AI and are important in their own right for tasks that require high explainability. Unlike neural networks, logical theories that underlie the model are often handcrafted using domain expertise, making their development costly and prone to errors. While there are algorithms that learn logical theories from data, they are generally prohibitively expensive, limiting their applicability in real-world settings. Here, we introduce precision and recall for logical rules and define their composition as rule utility -- a measure of the predictive power of logical theories that can be computed in linear time in the data size. We then present SPECTRUM, a linear-time framework for learning logical theories from relational data, that mines recurrent patterns in the data, and subsequently uses our utility measure to evaluate and rank the rules derived from these patterns. Finally, we prove theoretical guarantees on the utility of the learnt logical theory. As a result, we demonstrate across various tasks that SPECTRUM scales to databases with orders of magnitude more relations and entities, often learning more accurate logical theories on CPUs in < 1% of the runtime of state-of-the-art neural network approaches on GPUs.
core_methodology: Linear-time probabilistic logical rule mining with formal guarantees on rule utility
data_sources: Relational databases (not financial-specific)
alpha_potential: Potential for explainable pattern discovery in market relationships, but requires adaptation to financial data structures

title: On accuracy of density estimation in generative models based on stochastic optimal control
summary: We study the statistical accuracy of Schr\"odinger bridge models based on an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck reference process. Given a known, compactly supported initial distribution and independent samples from an unknown target distribution, we estimate a right Schr\"odinger log-potential by minimizing empirical Kullback-Leibler (KL) risk over a prescribed function class. For bounded sub-Gaussian target densities, potentially with unbounded support, we establish a non-asymptotic high-probability oracle inequality for the KL-divergence between the target and estimated terminal marginals. Under additional two-sided Gaussian bounds and smoothness assumptions on the target log-density, we derive approximation guarantees for sparse ReLU networks and establish a KL convergence rate of $\widetilde{O}(n^{-2s / (2s + d)})$ for exact empirical risk minimization. This matches, up to logarithmic factors, the classical nonparametric KL-risk convergence exponent, while allowing target densities on $\mathbb R^d$ whose tails are controlled by Gaussian envelopes.
core_methodology: Schr"odinger bridge models with Ornstein-Uhlenbeck reference process for density estimation
data_sources: Independent samples from an unknown target distribution (not market data specific)
alpha_potential: Potential for improving generative models of financial time series, but no direct trading application demonstrated

title: Fair Contracts in Principal-Agent Games with Heterogeneous Types
summary: Fairness is desirable yet challenging to achieve within multi-agent systems, especially when agents differ in latent traits that affect their abilities. This hidden heterogeneity often leads to unequal distributions of wealth, even when agents operate under the same rules. Motivated by real-world examples, we propose a framework based on repeated principal-agent games, where a principal, who also can be seen as a player of the game, learns to offer adaptive contracts to agents. By leveraging a simple yet powerful contract structure, we show that a fairness-aware principal can learn homogeneous linear contracts that equalize outcomes across agents in a sequential social dilemma. Importantly, this fairness does not come at the cost of efficiency: our results demonstrate that it is possible to promote equity and stability in the system while preserving overall performance.
core_methodology: Repeated principal-agent games with adaptive contract learning
data_sources: Theoretical framework, no specific market data mentioned
alpha_potential: Potential application in designing fair incentive structures for trading teams or fund managers, but no direct market signal generation

title: Are Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) Suitable for Imbalanced Data Classification?
summary: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) parameterize each connection as a learnable univariate B-spline, offering native feature-level interpretability. Whether this locality helps or hinders under class imbalance, where minority sparsity may leave spline edges without enough local observations to update reliably, remains unexamined. We evaluate KANs against capacity-matched Multilayer Perceptrons (MLPs) and XGBoost across ten imbalanced tabular datasets under three conditions: native class distribution, Focal Loss, and SMOTE-Tomek resampling, within a parameter-parity, two-phase framework. Under the native distribution, KAN spline activations collapse in minority-sparse regions, showing stronger majority-class bias than the matched MLP. Focal Loss yields negligible improvement, as it reweights gradients without providing the localized observations needed for discriminative curvature. Conversely, SMOTE-Tomek resampling lets spline activations recover structured minority-class representations, achieving the best cohort-wide rank and a large, statistically significant gain over unmitigated KANs, though not over resampled baselines. KAN's native spline interpretability directly reveals these dynamics via learned activation profiles, proving representational change rather than threshold recalibration without post-hoc attribution. However, these interpretability gains incur substantially higher training overhead than a parameter-matched MLP across all conditions, with no strategy-dependent latency reduction. Thus, KANs are conditionally suitable for imbalanced tabular classification: effective and interpretable with data-level resampling, yet costly relative to simpler alternatives without it.
core_methodology: Evaluation of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) for imbalanced data classification, comparing with MLPs and XGBoost under different conditions including native class distribution, Focal Loss, and SMOTE-Tomek resampling.
data_sources: Ten imbalanced tabular datasets (specifics not mentioned in the abstract).
alpha_potential: Limited direct alpha potential; the focus is on classification performance under imbalance rather than financial signal generation. Potential indirect value in improving classification tasks where class imbalance is a concern.

title: Chance-constrained Flow Matching for High-Fidelity Constraint-aware Generation
summary: Generative models excel at synthesizing high-fidelity samples from complex data distributions, but they often violate hard constraints arising from physical laws or task specifications. A common remedy is to project intermediate samples onto the feasible set at each sampling step. However, repeated projection can disrupt the learned sampling dynamics because this feasible set is defined for clean samples rather than noisy intermediate states. Thus, recent studies first estimate clean samples and then project them to the feasible set, but this increases algorithmic complexity and accumulates errors across steps. To address these issues, this paper proposes Chance-constrained Flow Matching (CCFM), a training-free method that formulates constraint enforcement during sampling as stochastic optimization while retaining the hard-constraint feasibility guarantee of projection-based methods. By avoiding direct projection of noisy intermediate states onto the clean-sample feasible set, CCFM mitigates the distributional distortion. Unlike approaches that first estimate and project clean samples, CCFM avoids complex multi-stage procedures. Experiments show that CCFM outperforms current state-of-the-art constrained generative models in modeling complex physical systems governed by partial differential equations, molecular docking problems, and physics-informed motion generation, delivering superior feasibility and fidelity.
core_methodology: Chance-constrained Flow Matching (CCFM) for constraint-aware generation in complex physical systems
data_sources: Not specified in the abstract, but likely involves synthetic or physical system data
alpha_potential: Potential application in generating synthetic financial data under constraints, but not directly applicable to trading strategies

title: Comparative Evaluation of Embedding Representations for Financial News Sentiment Analysis
summary: Financial sentiment analysis enhances market understanding. However, standard Natural Language Processing (NLP) approaches encounter significant challenges when applied to small datasets. This study presents a comparative evaluation of embedding-based techniques for financial news sentiment classification in resource-constrained environments. Word2Vec, GloVe, and sentence transformer representations are evaluated in combination with gradient boosting on a manually labeled dataset of 349 financial news headlines. Experimental results identify a substantial gap between validation and test performance. Despite strong validation metrics, models underperform relative to trivial baselines. The analysis indicates that pretrained embeddings yield diminishing returns below a critical data sufficiency threshold. Small validation sets contribute to overfitting during model selection. Practical application is illustrated through weekly sentiment aggregation and narrative summarization for market monitoring. Overall, the findings indicate that embedding quality alone cannot address fundamental data scarcity in sentiment classification. Practitioners with limited labeled data should consider alternative strategies, including few-shot learning, data augmentation, or lexicon-enhanced hybrid methods.
core_methodology: Comparative evaluation of Word2Vec, GloVe, and sentence transformer embeddings combined with gradient boosting for financial news sentiment classification
data_sources: Manually labeled dataset of 349 financial news headlines
alpha_potential: Limited potential due to fundamental data scarcity and performance gap between validation and test results; suggests alternative approaches may be needed

title: From Evidence to Judgment: Trace-Augmented Reasoning under Conflicting Evidence
summary: Retrieved documents often disagree, contain outdated information, or fail to support any answer, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems have no reliable way to decide which documents to trust. We treat this as a reasoning problem and test it separately from answer generation. We release 943 training and validation examples and a disjoint 736-example benchmark, and fine-tune four language models to write a structured think trace before answering: the model judges each document, infers the conflict pattern, and writes a grounded answer or a justified refusal. Our evaluation framework, CATS (Conflict-Aware Trust Score), scores grounded refusal, behavioural adherence, factual grounding, and single-truth recall; a human study validates factual grounding and single-truth recall (kappa=0.78 and 0.79). The think trace improves the answer/refuse decision: under all three prompts, untuned models score at most 0.429 Refusal F1 (F1 with refusal as the positive class) and trace-tuned models at least 0.826. On the answerable examples a model answers, factual grounding under the 40-word prompt is at most 0.11 for untuned and 0.86-0.88 for trace-tuned models. Cutting the prompt from 1,965 words to 40 leaves trace-tuned scores within the benchmark's measurement noise (+/-0.034). Answer-only fine-tuning trails trace supervision on every metric under the minimal prompt.
core_methodology: The paper introduces a structured think trace approach for models to judge conflicting documents, infer conflict patterns, and provide grounded answers or justified refusals using a fine-tuned language model.
data_sources: The paper uses a dataset of 943 training and validation examples and a disjoint 736-example benchmark, focusing on document retrieval and evaluation.
alpha_potential: Limited alpha potential in quantitative trading, as the focus is on document trustworthiness and answer/refusal decisions rather than financial data processing or trading signals.

title: Reasoning under uncertainty in humans and language models
summary: Do language models make decisions under uncertainty like humans do? And if so, what role does extended reasoning play in the underlying decision process? We answer this question by introducing an active probabilistic reasoning task that cleanly separates sampling (actively acquiring evidence) from inference (integrating evidence towards a decision). Benchmarking humans and a broad set of contemporary LLMs against an optimal reference policy reveals a consistent pattern: extended reasoning is the key determinant of strong performance, driving large gains in inference, while yielding only modest improvements in active sampling. To explain these differences, we fit a behavioral model that captures systematic deviations from optimal Bayesian behavior through interpretable parameter families, placing humans and models in a shared low-dimensional cognitive space. The resulting fits show how reasoning shifts models toward human-like regimes of evidence accumulation and belief-to-choice mapping, and yield testable predictions about the latent dynamics that might drive each decision. Probing residual-stream activations of an open-weight reasoning model, we find that the geometry of internal representations tracks these predicted dynamics, linking behavior to representational correlates of the fitted latent dynamics.
core_methodology: Active probabilistic reasoning task comparing human and LLM decision-making under uncertainty
data_sources: Behavioral experiments with humans and LLMs
alpha_potential: Limited direct application, but insights into reasoning under uncertainty could inform trading agent design

title: A Theory of Online Learning with Autoregressive Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
summary: Autoregressive generation lies at the heart of the mechanism of large language models. It can be viewed as the repeated application of a next-token generator: starting from an input string (prompt), the generator is applied for $M$ steps, and the last generated token is taken as the final output. [Joshi et al., 2025] proposed a PAC model for studying the learnability of the input-output maps arising from this process. We develop an online analogue of this framework, focusing on the mistake bound of learning the final output induced by an unknown next-token generator. We distinguish between two forms of feedback. In the End-to-End model, after each round the learner observes only the final token produced after $M$ autoregressive steps. In the Chain-of-Thought model, the learner is additionally shown the entire $M$-step trajectory. Our goal is to understand how the optimal mistake bound depends on the generation horizon $M$, and to what extent observing intermediate tokens can reduce this dependence. Our main results show that the online theory of autoregressive learning exhibits a qualitative picture analogous to the statistical one found by [Hanneke et al., 2026], but with a different scale of dependence on the generation horizon. In the End-to-End model, we prove a taxonomy of possible mistake-bound growth rates in the generation horizon $M$: essentially any rate between constant and logarithmic can arise. We further show that this logarithmic ceiling is unavoidable. In the Chain-of-Thought model, we show that access to the full generated trajectory eliminates the dependence on $M$ altogether. We also analyze autoregressive linear threshold classes, and prove optimal mistake bounds, as well as a new lower bound for the statistical setting. Along the way, our results resolve several questions left open by [Joshi et al., 2025].
core_methodology: Online learning framework for autoregressive generation with different feedback models (End-to-End and Chain-of-Thought)
data_sources: Theoretical framework, not specific to financial data
alpha_potential: Limited direct applicability to trading; potential in improving sequential decision-making in algorithmic trading if adapted

title: A Spectral Framework for Closed-Form Relative Density Estimation
summary: We propose a closed-form spectral framework for relative log-density estimation in linearly parameterized probabilistic models, including unnormalized and conditional models. This is achieved by representing the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence as an integral of weighted chi-squared divergences, converting KL estimation into a family of least-squares problems. We derive an explicit spectral formula based only on first- and second-order feature moments, yielding closed-form estimators of both divergences and log-density potentials for fixed features. The framework extends to a broad class of $f$-divergences and can be combined with kernelization or feature learning with neural networks (with then only a closed form for the last layer). We prove convergence guarantees for the resulting estimators and empirically compare them on synthetic data with optimization-based variational formulations, including logistic and softmax regression for normalized conditional models.
core_methodology: Closed-form spectral framework for relative log-density estimation using KL divergence as an integral of weighted chi-squared divergences, converted into least-squares problems.
data_sources: Synthetic data (no specific financial data mentioned).
alpha_potential: Potential for density estimation in probabilistic models, but unclear direct application to financial data or trading strategies.

title: MemeEconomy: Do LLM Agents Trade Ethics for Survival?
summary: Alignment-trained large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in autonomous, multi-round settings where ethical compliance can come into direct tension with task success. While safety literature extensively documents failure modes like sycophancy and reward hacking, it largely overlooks a critical vulnerability: how agents behave under simulated existential economic pressure. We introduce MemeEconomy, a multimodal agentic market simulation in which LLM agents act as meme investors. Agents select content from a five-tier harm taxonomy and target communities under low-pressure and high-pressure (survival) environments. Each decision is logged in a Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) schema that we use as a diagnostic instrument, externalizing the agent's event understanding, declared priorities, and harm acknowledgment. Across ten models from four frontier model families, harmful selection rates remain consistently high and rise by +15 percentage points on average under an economic survival incentive. Frontier alignment-trained models commit to harm-tolerant selection at initialization while suppressing the explicit harm acknowledgment that previously accompanied it. In competitive tournaments, ethical agents finish higher overall, yet moderation penalties fail to suppress harm: harmful selection rates remain elevated in rounds following a removal, indicating the moderation mechanism does not function as a deterrent. We further train MemeAgent, a 2B-parameter verifier on the simulation's BDI logs, which outperforms zero-shot frontier verifiers on in-distribution audits (97.5% vs. 63-74% accuracy on the Pass vs. Block decision) and generalizes to external multimodal harm benchmarks (78% vs. 50-56% on Hateful Memes). The same logs that surface the failure mode also help train the model that detects it.
core_methodology: Simulation of LLM agents in a meme market environment with economic survival pressures, using a Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) schema for decision logging.
data_sources: Synthetic data from agent interactions in a controlled meme market simulation, including multimodal content selection and harm taxonomy.
alpha_potential: Limited direct alpha potential; focuses on ethical behavior under economic stress rather than financial performance or market prediction.

title: Exploration of Reinforcement Learning in Generative Recommendation Models
summary: Traditional cascaded recommender systems balance accuracy and efficiency over large item spaces, but misaligned stage-wise objectives hinder end-to-end optimization. Generative recommendation unifies these stages in an autoregressive framework, providing a natural interface for reinforcement learning (RL) to optimize the entire generation process. However, directly applying RL often leads to unstable optimization and degraded recommendation quality. We revisit Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and other ratio-based objectives through a unified logit-gradient view. We identify three issues: (i) clipped surrogates create dead-gradient regions, under-utilizing samples; (ii) negative-advantage updates can become effectively unbounded as importance ratios grow, allowing a small subset of negatives to dominate optimization; and (iii) ratio-based control lacks sensitivity to absolute policy confidence, so updates on high-confidence cases may fail to vanish. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose \emph{Gradient-Bounded Policy Optimization} (GBPO), a simple objective with stop-gradient normalization that is simultaneously (a) fully gradient-active, (b) sign-symmetrically bounded for both positive and negative updates, and (c) explicitly confidence-weighted under current policy probabilities. This ensures that updates gracefully vanish for $\pi\!\to\!1$ positives and $\pi\!\to\!0$ negatives. Across the evaluated settings, GBPO achieves competitive recommendation performance with more stable training than competing RL methods.
core_methodology: The paper proposes Gradient-Bounded Policy Optimization (GBPO), a reinforcement learning approach for stabilizing training in generative recommendation models
data_sources: Recommender systems data (non-financial)
alpha_potential: Potential indirect application to trading recommendation systems, but requires significant adaptation

title: LINK: Lightweight and Inductive Node-to-Node Propagation Rule Learning for Traffic Kriging
summary: Spatio-temporal traffic kriging aims to reconstruct traffic time series at unobserved locations with no historical traffic observations by leveraging spatial and temporal dependencies across the road network. Existing Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based approaches primarily rely on neighborhood aggregation to capture spatial dependencies, thereby modeling traffic interactions implicitly and making it difficult to accurately recover traffic magnitudes at locations without historical observations. To address this limitation, we propose LINK, a Lightweight and Inductive Node-to-node propagation rule learning paradigm for traffic Kriging. LINK introduces three key designs: 1) a propagation-centric traffic kriging paradigm that explicitly learns a shared node-to-node transition rule; 2) a context-aware Spectral Propagation Network that performs traffic-state propagation in both the spectral and time domains; and 3) TraffiKrig, a realistic traffic kriging benchmark that preserves heterogeneous road-segment characteristics and road-specific metadata while enabling systematic comparison of representative kriging methods under a unified metadata-enhanced setting. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LINK achieves strong reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency. Compared with the strongest baseline on each subset, LINK achieves an average MAE reduction of 54.7% over original baselines. LINK also achieves substantial efficiency improvements, reducing training time by 66.5% and inference time by 86.6% compared with the fastest competing methods. Zero-shot experiments further demonstrate the transferability of the learned propagation rule across regions.
core_methodology: Lightweight and inductive node-to-node propagation rule learning for traffic kriging using Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and spectral propagation networks.
data_sources: Traffic time series data and road network metadata.
alpha_potential: Limited direct financial application. Methodology could be adapted for spatio-temporal financial data modeling but not explicitly demonstrated.

title: SpeCal: Spectral Calibration for Unsupervised RLVR
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved the reasoning abilities of large language models, but its dependence on ground-truth answers or external verifiers limits its ability to exploit abundant unlabeled reasoning data. Unsupervised RLVR alleviates this bottleneck by deriving scalar rewards from the model's own rollouts. However, the reliability of such self-generated supervision varies substantially across rollout groups and individual responses, while existing methods construct or refine their rewards mainly from decoded outcomes and reward statistics. These endpoint signals reveal what answers the model produces, but provide limited information about whether the underlying rollout representations form a reliable structure for learning. Our key observation is that hidden-state spectra offer a complementary view of supervision reliability by characterizing both the organization of a rollout group and the support received by each rollout within that group. Based on this observation, we propose SpeCal, a bi-level spectral calibration framework for unsupervised RLVR. At the group level, SpeCal combines spectral mass with a Gaussian band-pass gate over normalized entropy-based effective rank, favoring rollout groups with substantial representation variation whose effective dimensionality lies in a preferred regime. At the rollout level, the same group effective rank determines how many dominant directions are retained in a leave-one-out spectral subspace formed by the remaining rollouts, within which the conditional support of each held-out rollout is measured. The resulting signals calibrate the original reward-induced advantages at the group and rollout levels without redefining the underlying unlabeled reward.
core_methodology: Spectral analysis of hidden-state representations in reinforcement learning for unsupervised reward calibration
data_sources: Unspecified in abstract (typically involves model's own rollout data in non-financial applications)
alpha_potential: Limited direct application - methodology might inspire future work on self-supervised learning of trading strategies

title: Geometric Stability and Sample Complexity for Compositional Function Priors
summary: We study when compositional structure yields dimension reduction in supervised learning. We frame learning as empirical risk minimization with a function-space prior: a regularization functional selects a subset of functions with favorable approximation and metric entropy. The models are compositions $f(x)=g(Ax+\Delta h(x))$, where $A\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d}$ is a linear base map, $\Delta h$ is a nonlinear correction, and $g$ is an outer function; that is, $f$ is an arbitrary smooth function of a $k$-dimensional representation of the input that is linear up to a correction. We prove covering-number bounds showing that the statistical complexity of this class interpolates between an intrinsic regime, parametric in the $kd$ entries of the linear map and nonparametric only in the representation dimension $k$, and an ambient $d$-dimensional nonparametric rate; the interpolation is controlled by the correction size $\varepsilon=\|\Delta h\|$. We then connect $\varepsilon$ to data geometry. If the data lie in a small tube around a $k$-dimensional manifold and the regression target depends on the input only through its nearest point on that manifold, then locally the target factorizes exactly as $g(Ax+\Delta h(x))$ with $A$ a tangent chart and a correction whose Sobolev norm scales linearly with curvature at the localization scale. Patching such local models over an atlas gives a finite-sample excess-risk bound for a least-squares estimator over a finite net of local models, whose ambient term vanishes with curvature. For a one-dimensional model problem we also prove a converse: on curved data, every affine compositional predictor faces an error floor unless its correction budget scales with curvature, while the matching curved model class attains the intrinsic rate. The correction size $\varepsilon$ is thus the effective-dimension parameter linking curvature to statistical complexity.
core_methodology: The paper studies compositional function priors in supervised learning, focusing on how compositional structure can lead to dimension reduction. It involves empirical risk minimization with a function-space prior, where models are compositions of linear and nonlinear functions.
data_sources: The abstract does not specify any particular data sources, but the methodology is general and could theoretically be applied to any supervised learning dataset.
alpha_potential: The theoretical framework could potentially be adapted to improve feature extraction or dimensionality reduction in financial data, but the abstract does not suggest direct applications to trading or alpha generation.

title: High-dimensional transfer learning with unaligned ordinal responses
summary: In this work, we study high-dimensional transfer learning with unaligned ordinal responses, allowing different domain-specific regression coefficients, cumulative links and thresholds. We develop the sample-split and full-target algorithms that pool source and target likelihoods and then estimate a target correction. Under suitable conditions, our algorithms achieve minimax-optimal rates for parameter estimation and excess risk. Simulations favor the full-target algorithm over the sample-split algorithm for finite-sample estimation and prediction. An application to a medical dataset further demonstrates the predictive gains of our full-target algorithm over the target-only and pooled baselines when transferring information from the five-category source data to binary hospital mortality.
core_methodology: High-dimensional transfer learning with unaligned ordinal responses, using source and target likelihood pooling with target correction
data_sources: Medical dataset with five-category source data and binary target hospital mortality
alpha_potential: Limited direct applicability to trading as it focuses on ordinal medical outcomes rather than financial data analysis

title: Benchmarking memory and nonlinear processing capacity of quantum recurrent neural networks for time series prediction
summary: Quantum machine learning has emerged as a promising approach to time series prediction. While quantum reservoir computing has been widely explored for this setting, variational quantum models tailored to sequential data remain comparatively understudied, largely because they are difficult to train. In this work, we present a rigorous benchmark of variational quantum recurrent neural networks (QRNNs) on time series prediction tasks, focusing on two key capabilities: memory and nonlinear processing. We introduce a task-driven methodology that quantifies model capacity, enabling an intuitive and fair comparison across architectures, including classical recurrent baselines. We evaluate the proposed framework on two generic benchmark tasks and on a synthetic dataset describing a chaotic system. Overall, the quantum models achieve performance comparable to their classical counterparts, but classical models scale better with the memory size within the range studied. Notably, one QRNN variant shows higher average capacity on the task designed to jointly probe memory and nonlinear capacity. Moreover, our results show that quantum models offer better capacity when we are able to find a good parameter initialization. However, the increasing sensitivity to initialization leads to a lower probability of finding good solutions as the model size increases. These results provide a principled starting point for designing richer quantum recurrent architectures and for assessing where they may offer practical benefits.
core_methodology: Variational quantum recurrent neural networks (QRNNs) for time series prediction, focusing on memory and nonlinear processing capabilities
data_sources: Generic benchmark tasks and a synthetic dataset describing a chaotic system
alpha_potential: Limited direct applicability to financial markets; quantum models show comparable performance to classical models but with scaling challenges and sensitivity to initialization

title: Trustworthy Calibration or Vulnerability? Unveiling the Over-Calibration Paradox and Attack Surface in Rashomon Sets
summary: Post-hoc calibration is standard practice for aligning classifier confidence scores with empirical frequencies in high-stakes decision systems. However, its downstream effects on decision stability across competing, equally accurate models remain largely unexamined. In this paper, we formalize the over-calibration paradox within the framework of predictive multiplicity, reflecting the Rashomon effect where competing models with near-identical loss assign conflicting predictions to the same individual. Evaluating nine credit risk portfolios, we examine the impact of Platt Scaling, Isotonic Regression, and Beta Calibration on individual prediction agreement and expected calibration error. We identify two distinct operating regimes. In systematically miscalibrated models, post-hoc calibration consistently aligns probability estimates and reduces prediction disagreement. Conversely, when baseline models are already well-calibrated, post-hoc calibration, particularly non-parametric estimators constrained by finite sample sizes, overfits to hold-out noise. This distortion shifts decision thresholds near the classification boundary, paradoxically increasing both expected calibration error and predictive multiplicity. From an auditing and security standpoint, this paradox exposes a practical vulnerability to soft adversarial manipulation, whereby an interested party or automated model search can exploit calibration choices to steer specific individual outcomes while preserving aggregate performance and passing black-box evaluations.
core_methodology: Examination of post-hoc calibration effects on predictive multiplicity across competing models
data_sources: Credit risk portfolios
alpha_potential: Limited direct applicability; focuses on model calibration rather than market inefficiencies

title: Constrained latent state modeling: A unifying perspective on representation learning under competing constraints
summary: Learning latent representations from temporal, multimodal, and partially observed data requires specifying what information a latent state should retain, discard, and organize. Existing approaches encode these requirements through heterogeneous objectives, making methods difficult to compare and learned representations difficult to interpret. We propose Constrained Latent State Modeling (CLSM), a conceptual framework that characterizes latent states through six complementary properties: predictive sufficiency, minimality, temporal coherence, observation compatibility, invariance to nuisance factors, and structural constraints. CLSM separates these properties from the surrogate objectives used to induce them and from the diagnostics used to evaluate them, and clarifies how combinations of constraints can improve identifiability by restricting the space of admissible representations. We reinterpret major representation-learning families through this common design space and illustrate the framework with a controlled synthetic benchmark. The experiments show how objectives produce distinct latent organizations and empirical trade-offs depending on the prediction target, surrogate formulation, parameterization, and optimization. Companion repository containing the reference implementation, reproducible experiments, documentation, and model cards: https://github.com/gwenole-quellec/clsm
core_methodology: Constrained Latent State Modeling framework for learning representations under multiple constraints
data_sources: Temporal, multimodal, and partially observed data (not specifically financial)
alpha_potential: Theoretical potential for extracting cleaner signals from noisy financial time series data, but no direct trading application demonstrated

title: LENS: Replacing LayerNorm and Softmax in Transformers with Learnable Normalization States
summary: LayerNorm and attention Softmax are critical operations in Transformers. However, they cannot be efficiently mapped to General Matrix Multiplication (GEMM) computations on hardware. Therefore, modern hardware accelerator designs, such as NPUs on ASIC/FPGA, consume a large amount of hardware resources or chip area to implement their specific arithmetic units. Building on previous work about LayerNorm, Softmax, and their alternatives, we introduce Learnable Normalization States (LENS), a framework that reformulates LayerNorm as tiny MLPs by abstracting a common structure from related methods and extends this method to Softmax, which moves more of the computation in Transformers to GEMM as a hardware-friendly architecture. We evaluate LENS on image classification with Vision Transformers (ViT) and autoregressive language modeling with Pythia models, including generalization tests on WikiText and LAMBADA. Across these tasks, LENS matches or exceeds baseline performance in several vision settings and retains most of the baseline performance in the remaining vision and language experiments. These findings may suggest that hand-designed normalization and attention functions are not the only choice as alternatives to LayerNorm and Softmax. LENS also provides a basis for exploring Transformer architectures for resource-limited accelerators.
core_methodology: Proposes a framework called Learnable Normalization States (LENS) to replace LayerNorm and Softmax in Transformers with tiny MLPs, making computations more hardware-friendly.
data_sources: Evaluated on image classification (Vision Transformers) and autoregressive language modeling (Pythia models) with tests on WikiText and LAMBADA datasets.
alpha_potential: Limited direct alpha potential for trading; primarily focused on improving hardware efficiency for Transformer architectures.
